digest.intro: Ice melts, blood becomes brain, and Serbia elects scientists to parliament.

items.title: Iran, Ukraine, and the Shape of Simultaneous Crises
items.blurb: The week's real story isn't any single event but the interaction among three unresolved crises: an Iran war straining U.S. military reach and energy markets, a fragile Ukraine ceasefire effort, and Indo-Pacific competition intensifying beneath it all. On Iran specifically, Qatari mediators presented a seven-day confidence-building framework that Tehran immediately rejected — not just over terms, but over the sequencing of who moves first. That disagreement about the order of concessions is the actual wall.

items.title: Serbia Just Elected the World's Brainiest Parliament
items.blurb: Serbian voters swept scientists into a parliamentary supermajority — not a technocrat-adjacent business class, but working researchers and academics. The structural story underneath is about what happens when institutional trust collapses so completely that credentialed outsiders become the only legible alternative to career politicians. Worth watching as a live experiment in whether expertise-as-mandate actually governs differently, or just wears a different costume.

items.title: A Wireless Implant That Converts Blood Sugar Into Something the Kidneys Can Flush
items.blurb: ETH Zurich and French collaborators built a wireless electronic device — paired to a continuous glucose monitor — that activates automatically when glucose spikes and catalyzes the conversion of excess sugar into gluconate, which the kidneys clear. In mouse trials over six weeks it normalized blood glucose and reduced body weight by 10%, the latter because the body compensates by burning fat. Still in animals, but the mechanism is genuinely different from anything currently in the clinic.

items.title: Procedural Botanical Geometry in LaTeX — Every Page Gets Its Own Garden
items.blurb: Someone went completely down the rabbit hole on procedural Delft-blue floral margins for LaTeX documents: no images, no imported paths, every petal and stem a parametric curve computed in Lua at render time using a space-filling layout borrowed from a 1998 ornament paper. The seed changes per page, so the garden is never the same twice. There's a browser playground that outputs SVG, LaTeX preamble, or Typst — the kind of obsessive narrow craft that's genuinely beautiful to look at.

items.title: The Oldest Ice Is Melting and the Stone Age Is Walking Out of It
items.blurb: For 20 years, glacial archaeologists in Norway's Innlandet mountains have been recovering artifacts from melting ice — mostly Viking Age material up to 2,000 years old. But now the ancient ice is going, and what's inside it is older: this season alone they recovered 48 prehistoric arrows, including a 5,000–6,000-year-old slate-tipped arrow with its shaft still intact. Organic material — wood, leather, textiles — survived perfectly in the ice. The past is literally surfacing through climate change in real time.

items.title: This Material Sorts Itself
items.blurb: Steve Mould on the Brazil nut effect — the counterintuitive phenomenon where shaking a mixed granular system causes larger particles to rise, spontaneously sorting by size without any external direction. Mould is unusually good at making emergent physical behavior visually legible; this one has implications for thinking about self-organization in any system that looks disordered but isn't.

facts.fact: In a six-week mouse trial, an implanted wireless device lowered blood glucose and reduced body weight by 10% — purely by converting excess sugar into a kidney-clearable compound, with no drugs involved.

Norwegian glacial archaeologists recovered 48 prehistoric arrows in a single field season — including a slate-tipped arrow estimated at 5,000–6,000 years old — as ancient ice that had never melted in recorded history finally gives way.

The Florilegium LaTeX package generates every petal, leaf, and stem as a parametric curve computed in Lua at compile time — no images, no imported paths — and uses a space-filling algorithm from a 1998 ornament paper to populate margins differently on every page.

Iran rejected a Qatari-mediated seven-day confidence-building framework not primarily over its terms, but over the sequencing — who makes the first concession — which diplomats identified as the central structural obstacle to any settlement.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film that works like a mind: associative, obsessive, deeply interested in how images and memory build the reality we inhabit. Marker wanders from Tokyo to Guinea-Bissau treating culture as a living system — ritual, symbol, feedback loop — and the whole thing is held together by sheer craft and curiosity. If you care about how surfaces encode meaning, this one never stops giving.

art_picks.title: The Unilever Series: Olafur Eliasson — The Weather Project
art_picks.creator: Olafur Eliasson
art_picks.why: The canonical example of a physical environment that hacks perception and social behavior simultaneously — thousands of strangers lying on a museum floor staring at a mirror ceiling, performing their own awe back at themselves. The technology was simple; the feedback loop it created between architecture, light, and human behavior was genuinely strange. Eliasson's studio page stays current with where that thinking has gone.

art_picks.title: Daphne Oram — Individual Homage (Oramics works)
art_picks.creator: Daphne Oram
art_picks.why: Oram built her own synthesizer from scratch in 1957 — a machine that read shapes she drew directly on 35mm film — because no existing instrument could make the sounds she heard in her head. The resulting pieces feel less like compositions than diagrams of an interior world. Someone going unreasonably deep on one narrow, self-invented thing: this is the apex of that.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt — Last Chance
events.venue: Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), Midtown Manhattan
events.why: Huyghe feeds AI dream-reconstructions of neural signals into a living installation with sensors, screens, and sound — a system that perceives its viewers while they perceive it; it's the physical/digital edge at its most philosophically loaded, and it closes at the end of November.

events.name: Rashid Johnson: Birthday Boys — Opening
events.why: Johnson's openings consistently function as a kind of living scene — his work operates at the intersection of Black identity, mythology, material systems, and anxiety — and Hauser & Wirth's Tribeca space is worth showing up to on its own terms.

events.name: Art Week NYC — Inaugural Edition
events.venue: Citywide (Chelsea, Tribeca, LES, UES + New Museum hub at 235 Bowery)
events.why: The first-ever citywide contemporary art festival organized by Artforum, ARTnews, and Art in America, uniting 76+ galleries and 32 institutions — culminating in a day of public talks at the newly expanded New Museum on topics including machine intelligence in studio practice and the economics of making art in New York; not a fair, more like a curated city-scale argument about what contemporary art is right now.

events.name: Sting 3.0 Tour — Intimate Run at Brooklyn Paramount
events.why: Sting's stripped-back power trio (with Dominic Miller and Chris Maas) doing eight nights in a beautifully restored 3,000-cap theater — not a nostalgia arena tour but a consciously intimate format in a room with real sound; the Nov 11–14 dates fall in the window and several include Fiction Plane as support.

events.name: James Turrell: Something Old, Something New, Something Borrowed, Something Blue
events.why: A Turrell gallery show opening during Art Week NYC — light as the sole medium, perception as the subject, and the title suggests a conceptual game with inheritance and novelty that goes beyond his usual Skyspace solemnity.
